title: Europe missed the AI labs but is winning the toolshed
excerpt: Europe’s established tech and industrial giants have emerged as unexpected winners of the AI boom, even as the continent lacks a frontier lab of its own.
content_html:
Europe missed out on building the AI labs, and is quietly cashing in anyway. The continent’s established tech and industrial giants have emerged as unexpected winners of the AI boom, according to Reuters, even as its startups struggle to rival OpenAI or Google.

The pattern is a lesson in where the money actually lands. Frontier models grab the headlines, but the profits also flow to the companies that make the tools, run the software, and wire the power, and Europe is unusually strong in all three.

The clearest case is ASML, the Dutch firm whose lithography machines are the only way to make the most advanced AI chips, and which has been closing on a trillion-dollar valuation as demand surges.

Enterprise software is the other engine. SAP, now among Europe’s most valuable companies, sells the systems that big firms are wiring AI into, and every AI feature it adds is one more reason for customers to stay.

Then there is the unglamorous business of power and metal. Siemens has raised its outlook on AI-driven data-centre demand, and electrical firms such as Schneider and Prysmian are riding the buildout that every data centre requires.

The mechanism is straightforward; every dollar spent training a model eventually reaches a chip, and every advanced chip passes through an ASML machine, so the spending that starts in California ends up, in part, in the Netherlands.

Telecoms and utilities benefit too as data centres need connectivity and vast amounts of power, and the European firms that provide both are booking the demand whether or not a single European model competes at the frontier.

That this counts as a surprise says a lot about the narrative. Europe has spent two years being told it lost the AI race, a story that measured the continent only by whether it had produced its own ChatGPT.

By that measure it did fall behind. Europe has fretted openly about its AI sovereignty, dependent on American models and clouds for the frontier work its own firms cannot yet match.

There are exceptions like Mistral, the French champion, who has finally started to make its sovereignty bet pay, but a single lab does not close a gap this wide.

The incumbents’ advantage is that they do not need to win the model race to profit from it. In a gold rush, selling picks and shovels has always been the steadier business, and Europe happens to own much of the hardware store.

Collaborative efforts are trying to fill the rest. A pan-European alliance has built an open LLM as an alternative to American and Chinese models, though it remains a modest counterweight to the giants.

The win is real but narrow. It rests on selling into a boom the incumbents do not control, and if the AI build-out slows, demand for their tools and power slows with it.

It has also reshuffled Europe’s corporate hierarchy. The most valuable companies on the continent are increasingly its AI-adjacent industrials and toolmakers, rather than its banks or luxury houses.

The gains are unevenly spread, too. They cluster in chip tools, industrial software, and electrification, while Europe’s consumer-internet and social platforms remain as absent from the AI story as ever.

For policymakers, the result is awkward. Europe is profiting from AI while remaining dependent on others for the intelligence itself, a comfortable position that is also a fragile one.

The danger is reading the profits as a strategy. Selling into someone else’s boom is lucrative until the buyer builds its own supply, and Europe’s dependence on foreign models is a vulnerability a strong quarter does not fix.

Still, being the toolshed to a global boom is not the worst place to stand. Europe may not have built the future of AI, but it is selling a great deal of what that future runs on.

content_html_zh:
欧洲错过了建设人工智能实验室的机会，但无论如何，它正在悄悄地获利。 据路透社报道，尽管非洲大陆的初创公司难以与 OpenAI 或谷歌竞争，但非洲大陆成熟的科技和工业巨头已成为人工智能热潮的意外赢家。

这种模式是一个教训，让我们了解资金的实际落脚点。 前沿模型占据了头条新闻，但利润也流向了制造工具、运行软件和布线的公司，而欧洲在这三方面都异常强大。

最明显的例子是荷兰公司 ASML，其光刻机是制造最先进人工智能芯片的唯一方法，随着需求激增，该公司的估值已接近万亿美元。

企业软件是另一个引擎。 SAP 现在是欧洲最有价值的公司之一，销售大公司将人工智能连接到其中的系统，它添加的每一项人工智能功能都是客户留下来的又一个理由。

然后是乏味的电力和金属行业。 西门子提高了对人工智能驱动的数据中心需求的展望，施耐德和普睿司曼等电力公司正在利用每个数据中心所需的扩建。

该机制很简单；训练模型所花费的每一美元最终都会到达芯片，而每一个先进的芯片都会经过 ASML 机器，因此从加利福尼亚开始的支出最终会部分流向荷兰。

电信和公用事业也受益，因为数据中心需要连接和大量电力，而提供这两者的欧洲公司正在预订需求，无论单一欧洲模式是否在前沿竞争。

这算得上是一个惊喜，这充分说明了故事的内容。 欧洲已经花了两年的时间被告知它输掉了人工智能竞赛，这个故事只能通过是否产生了自己的 ChatGPT 来衡量欧洲大陆。

按照这个标准，它确实落后了。 欧洲公开担心其人工智能主权，依赖美国的模式和云技术来开展其自己的公司尚无法匹敌的前沿工作。

也有一些例外，比如法国冠军米斯特拉尔 (Mistral)，它终于开始让自己的主权赌注得到回报，但单个实验室无法缩小如此大的差距。

现有企业的优势在于，他们不需要赢得模特比赛就能从中获利。 在淘金热时期，销售镐和铲子一直是比较稳定的生意，而欧洲恰好拥有大部分五金店。

共同努力正在努力填补剩下的空白。 一个泛欧洲联盟已经建立了一个开放的法学硕士课程，作为美国和中国模式的替代方案，尽管它仍然是对巨头的适度制衡。

胜利是真实的，但差距有限。 它依赖于现有企业无法控制的繁荣，如果人工智能建设放缓，对其工具和电力的需求也会随之放缓。

它还重新洗牌了欧洲的企业层级。 非洲大陆最有价值的公司越来越多地是与人工智能相关的工业和工具制造商，而不是银行或奢侈品牌。

收益分布也不均匀。 它们集中在芯片工具、工业软件和电气化领域，而欧洲的消费互联网和社交平台仍然在人工智能的故事中缺席。

对于政策制定者来说，结果是尴尬的。 欧洲正在从人工智能中获利，但智能本身仍然依赖其他国家，这是一种舒适的处境，但同时也是脆弱的。

危险在于将利润视为一种策略。 在买家建立自己的供应之前，在其他国家的繁荣时期出售产品是有利可图的，而欧洲对外国模式的依赖是一个强劲的季度无法修复的弱点。

尽管如此，成为全球繁荣的工具库并不是最糟糕的处境。 欧洲可能没有构建人工智能的未来，但它正在出售大量未来运行的产品。
